title: Your automated playtests are lying to you - add Fitts's law
author: p0w3rm0r3
selftext:
Most of us run automated playtests or simulations to balance a game. The simulated player "clicks" instantly and perfectly: it teleports to the button, never misses, and reads a 60-word card in zero seconds. A human doesn't do any of that.  
**Fitts's law** says the time to hit a target grows with distance and shrinks with target size:  
T = a + b \* log2(D / W + 1)  
where D is the distance to the target and W is its width. Typical values are a ≈ 0.1-0.2 s and b ≈ 0.1-0.15 s/bit. On top of that comes reaction time (\~250 ms) and reading time (\~200-250 words per minute).  
I added this to the simulated player in my strategy game. It now moves a virtual cursor along a path, misses small targets now and then, waits a moment before reacting, and "reads" text before deciding. Then I compared it with the instant version on the same seeds:  
First buildings came 0.3-1.1 in-game days later. That's not huge, but it's measurable.  
My Build button was 930-1400 px from where the action happens. The instant player never noticed. With pressing B to open the build menu at the cursor, the travel dropped to 120-160 px per placement.  
The biggest find was a bug no instant simulation could catch: notification cards at the bottom centre of the screen covered exactly the spot where you drag roads. The "human" player made 51 road attempts and built 0 roads, because the clicks landed on the cards. The instant player clicked through the same spot fine, because it never checked what was under the cursor.  
Decision cards took 10-13 s to read. The instant player read them for free.  
**TL;DR:** if your simulation doesn't pay for distance, target size, reaction and reading, it measures your game logic, not your game. It's about 200 lines of code, and it found UI problems I'd have shipped.  
Curious if anyone else simulates input cost in their automated tests, or does everyone rely on real playtesters for this?

comments.author: Felmeric
comments.body:
I didn't know there was a formula for this sort of thing but I did run into the same issue when working on my game. 

Claude told me things were possible but when I tried to play test the same part I couldn't do it, no matter how hard I tried. When I asked about it, it revealed the testing it was doing was all instant, pixel perfect, 0 reaction time. I had to tell it to add very generous margins in f
or human players and then it was able to find that most of the things were impossible for a human. 

I'll try to remember this for next time.

comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
I feel like I’m missing something. If I read you right, you had a UI issue where notifications blocked the build button until read. Claude read them instantly, clicked Build instantly, reported all good, and you caught the problem yourself.

…is this not the type of thing you immediately notice when playtesting your own game? Your question at the end asks about “real playtesters” and I can’t help but think “yeah, myself” lol.

replies.author: p0w3rm0r3
replies.body: I am playtesting but in one case I let Claude do the first run and found this UI problem.

replies.author: NeusomaDev
replies.body:
Gotcha, yeah, to me this highlights the division of labor for playtesting more than anything. My shooter does a shitload of automated testing for things like whether movement or hit registration hold up under simulated lag, or what my frame times are under different conditions, etc. I’ve found that works well once I set the bounds for “this is the target latency,” “this is the maximum acceptable,” and the like, but I don’t think Claude would have ever been able to make those judgments itself, because it can’t “feel” whether different lag levels are good or bad.

Fitts’s law seems like a useful concept to know for UI/UX design for sure though. And I didn’t, before now, so thanks for sharing!

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body: Same kind of problem from my jam game, one layer lower. The bots didn't just click instantly, they skipped input entirely and called the attack in code, so 227 tests passed while real mouse clicks almost never reached the sword. The fix was a check that posts real mouse-down and mouse-up messages to the game window and counts what arrives. It doesn't model human timing like yours does, but at least the clicks go through the same path a player's do.
